To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cigarette smoking is associated with a 30-fold increased number of Langerhans (LC) cells present in the al-veolar parench-yma.
cigarette smoking increases the number, distribution and differentiated state of cells belonging to the DC/LC lineage in the human lung.

cigarette smoking increases the total number of pulmonary dendritic/Langerhans cell lineage cells in the lung, and that this increase is largely due to an expansion of the number of Langerhans-like cells in the alveoli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of cigarette smoke on the immune system of smokers.
the effects of cigarette smoking on pulmonary DC/LC and the role of these cells in Langerhans' cell granulomatous inflammation.
the effects of smoking and air pollutants on the human lung.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cigarette smoking induces a marked increase in the number and distribution of cells of DC and LC lineage in the alveoli, but not in the bronchioli.
cigarette smoking is associated with an increase in the total numbers of LC and DC in the alveoli of the human lung.

cigarette smoke induces a marked increase in the number and differentiation of pulmonary DC/LC, which may explain, at least in part, why most adult patients with Langerhans granulomatosis have a history of cigarette smoking.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cigarette smoking causes an increase in the number, distribution and differentiated state of LC in the lung, which may explain, in part, the increased risk for developing Langerhans Cell Granulomatosis in smokers.
cigarette smoke induces an expansion and migration of LC from the bronchiolar to the alveolar epithelium and that this migration may occur via a process of type II pneumocyte differentiation.
cigarette smoking induces an increase in the number and a change in the distribution of LC in the lung.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cigarette smoking is associated with an increase in the total and alveolar number of DC/LC, and the majority of LC are found in the alveoli in close association with alveolar type 2 pneumocyte hyperplastic foci.
cigarette smoking is associated with an increase in the number and differentiation of DC/LC in the alveoli, which may be related to the development of Langerhans Cell Granulomatosis in smokers.
cigarette smoke is associated with an increase in the number and distribution of cells of the dendritic/Langerhans cell lineage in the lung.
